The "Conservation and Adaptive Reuse of Fujian Tulou" exhibition at the City of Architecture and Heritage in Paris showcases the remarkable architectural heritage of these unique Chinese communal dwellings. The Fujian Tulou, inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage sites in 2008, are large earthen buildings that have housed entire clans of Hakka people for centuries.

The exhibition highlights the innovative construction techniques used in these structures, which feature rammed earth walls up to 1.5 meters thick, creating natural insulation that keeps the interior cool in summer and warm in winter. The circular or square-shaped buildings, typically three to five stories high, are arranged around a central courtyard that serves as a communal space.

The adaptive reuse portion of the exhibition demonstrates how these historical structures are being transformed for contemporary use while preserving their cultural significance. Several successful cases are presented, including the conversion of tulous into boutique hotels, cultural centers, and museums.

The exhibition includes detailed architectural models, photographs, and multimedia installations that explain the traditional building techniques. Of particular interest is the display showing how the wooden framework is integrated with the earthen walls, using a unique mortise and tenon joinery system developed during the Ming Dynasty.

The construction materials section reveals that the walls are composed of a mixture of clay, sand, and rice husks, with bamboo strips added for reinforcement. This traditional mixture has proven remarkably durable, with some tulous surviving more than six centuries of use under harsh weather conditions.

The exhibition also features the work of renowned architect Wang Shu, who incorporated tulou-inspired elements into his modern designs throughout eastern China. His innovative approach to combining traditional techniques with contemporary architecture earned him recognition from the Royal Institute of British Architects in 1998, making him the first Asian architect to receive their prestigious Gold Medal.

Recent preservation efforts highlighted in the exhibition show how local communities have adapted traditional lime-based coatings with modern waterproofing compounds to protect these structures from deterioration. The success of these conservation methods has led to their adoption at other earthen architecture sites across Southeast Asia, particularly in Vietnam's ancient temple complexes.

The "Conservation and Adaptive Reuse of Fujian Tulou" exhibition at the Cité de l'Architecture et du Patrimoine in France offers a fascinating exploration into the adaptation and preservation of these unique structures from southeastern China. Fujian Tulou are traditional circular houses constructed using a blend of cement and steel, designed to withstand attacks and environmental challenges. These robust multi-story buildings typically housed up to 20 families and served as a communal living space.

The exhibition delves into the innovative reuse of Tulou buildings, showcasing their transformation into modern eco-friendly hotels and art galleries. Special attention is given to the 15th-century origins of these structures, highlighting their architectural evolution over the centuries from fortress-like dwellings into elegant, sophisticated buildings that bear European and Islamic architectural influences. The Tulou’s distinctive style, characterized by round and oval shapes, is also linked to the influence of the Tang dynasty, rather than their original regional inspirations. Visitors are introduced to conservation techniques using traditional bamboo reinforcement, illustrating a fusion of ancient knowledge and contemporary practices in preserving these World Heritage Sites.

The "Conservation and Adaptive Reuse of Fujian Tulou" exhibition at the City of Architecture and Heritage in France highlights the innovative architecture and sustainable practices of the Fujian Tulou, traditional Chinese rural dwellings primarily found in the Fujian province. These structures are known for their circular design, often standing several stories tall, and traditionally constructed from bamboo and mud bricks. Fujian Tulou have a unique historical significance as they were built during the Qin Dynasty and served as fortified village complexes for the Hakka people.

This exhibition showcases various aspects of Tulou architecture, including their role as communal living spaces for up to 500 families each. Additionally, it explores the adaptive reuse of these structures, turning some into contemporary museums and luxury hotels while maintaining their original makeup without adding modern materials. The exhibition also highlights the environmental benefits of Tulou architecture, such as their ability to maintain a stable internal temperature due to their thick walls, which serve as an early example of passive solar design. Hence, these buildings represent both an architectural marvel and an embodiment of sustainable living practices used for centuries in China.
